questions.question: Where did the ceremonies take place? Can you name any public buildings in India that are made of sandstone?
answer_steps: In the sandstone amphitheatre of the Union Buildings in Pretoria.
Sandstone buildings in India: the Red Fort, Rashtrapati Bhavan, Parliament House (Sansad Bhavan).

questions.question: Can you say how 10 May is an 'autumn day' in South Africa?
answer_steps: South Africa is in the southern hemisphere, where the seasons are opposite to India's.
So May, which is summer in India, falls in autumn there.

questions.question: At the beginning of his speech, Mandela mentions 'an extraordinary human disaster'. What does he mean by this?
answer_steps: He means apartheid, the system of racial discrimination.
Black people were denied rights and dignity for a very long time.

questions.question: What is the 'glorious... human achievement' he speaks of at the end?
answer_steps: The end of apartheid and the setting up of a democratic, non-racial government.
A Black man becoming President of a country that once denied Black people their rights.

questions.question: What does Mandela thank the international leaders for?
answer_steps: For coming to the inauguration and sharing the victory for justice, peace and human dignity.
For their support to the people of South Africa during the struggle.

questions.question: What ideals does he set out for the future of South Africa?
answer_steps: To free all people from poverty, deprivation, suffering, gender and other discrimination.
That the land should never again know the oppression of one by another: 'Let freedom reign.'

questions.question: What did the military generals do? How did their attitude change, and why?
answer_steps: They saluted Mandela and pledged their loyalty.
Years before they would have arrested him; the long struggle and many sacrifices brought democracy and changed their attitude.

questions.question: Why were two national anthems sung?
answer_steps: To show respect for both the white and the Black communities.
The whites sang 'Nkosi Sikelel–iAfrika' and the blacks sang 'Die Stem', a sign of unity.

questions.question: How does Mandela describe the systems of government in his country (i) in the first decade, and (ii) in the final decade, of the twentieth century?
answer_steps: (i) A system of racial domination by white people over dark-skinned people.
(ii) A system that recognised the rights and freedoms of all, whatever the colour of their skin.

questions.question: What does courage mean to Mandela? Which does he think is natural, to love or to hate?
answer_steps: Courage is not the absence of fear but the triumph over it.
He thinks love comes more naturally to the human heart than hate.

questions.question: What 'twin obligations' does Mandela mention?
answer_steps: Obligations to his family: parents, wife and children.
Obligations to his people, community and country.

questions.question: What did being free mean to Mandela as a boy, and as a student?
answer_steps: As a boy: to run in the fields, swim in streams, roast mealies and ride bulls.
As a student: to stay out at night, read what he pleased and go where he chose.

questions.question: Does Mandela think the oppressor is free? Why/Why not?
answer_steps: No.
The oppressor is a prisoner of hatred, locked behind the bars of prejudice and narrow-mindedness.

questions.question: Why did such a large number of international leaders attend the inauguration? What did it signify?
answer_steps: Leaders from more than 140 countries came to show support for the end of apartheid and the new democracy.
It signified the world's recognition of the victory of justice, peace and human dignity in South Africa.

questions.question: What does Mandela mean when he says he is 'simply the sum of all those African patriots' who had gone before him?
answer_steps: He gives credit to the many freedom fighters who struggled and sacrificed before him.
His achievement rests on their courage; he sees himself as the continuation of their struggle.

questions.question: Would you agree that the 'depths of oppression' create 'heights of character'? How does Mandela illustrate this? Can you add your own examples?
answer_steps: Yes: apartheid produced leaders of great courage and generosity such as Oliver Tambo, Walter Sisulu and Chief Luthuli.
Indian examples: Mahatma Gandhi and Bhagat Singh grew great through the struggle against British rule.

questions.question: How did Mandela's understanding of freedom change with age and experience?
answer_steps: As a boy, freedom meant playing freely; as a student, staying out late and reading what he liked.
As a young man he wanted the basic freedoms of earning a living and raising a family; then he saw that his people were not free and fought for their freedom.

questions.question: How did Mandela's 'hunger for freedom' change his life?
answer_steps: His hunger for his own freedom became a hunger for the freedom of his people.
It made a frightened young man bold, a lawyer a 'criminal', and a family man homeless, leading to years in prison.

questions.question:
Read the extract and answer the questions.

*Tenth May dawned bright and clear. For the past few days I had been pleasantly besieged by dignitaries and world leaders*
*who were coming to pay their respects before the inauguration.*
*The inauguration would be the largest gathering ever of international leaders on South African soil.*

(i) Who is 'I' in the extract?

(ii) Why does he call 10 May a special day?

(iii) Find a word that means 'surrounded'.

(iv) Why does he say 'pleasantly' besieged?

(v) What did the large gathering show?
answer_steps: (i) Nelson Mandela.
(ii) It was the day of his inauguration as President.
(iii) Besieged.
(iv) He was happy to meet the leaders who had come to honour him.
(v) The world's support for the new democracy.

questions.question:
Read the extract and answer the questions.

*A few moments later we all lifted our eyes in awe as a spectacular array of South African jets, helicopters and troop carriers*
*roared in perfect formation over the Union Buildings.*
*It was not only a display of pinpoint precision and military force, but a demonstration of the military's loyalty to democracy.*

(i) Where did the planes fly?

(ii) Give a word from the extract that means 'wonder and respect'.

(iii) What did the display demonstrate?

(iv) Why was this significant?

(v) Which phrase shows the flying was exact?
answer_steps: (i) Over the Union Buildings in Pretoria.
(ii) Awe.
(iii) The military's loyalty to democracy.
(iv) A few years earlier the army would have arrested Mandela.
(v) 'Pinpoint precision' / 'perfect formation'.

questions.question:
Read the extract and answer the questions.

*I learned that courage was not the absence of fear, but the triumph over it.*
*The brave man is not he who does not feel afraid, but he who conquers that fear.*

(i) Who learned this lesson?

(ii) From whom did he learn it?

(iii) What is courage, according to the extract?

(iv) Give the antonym of 'absence'.

(v) Which word means 'defeats'?
answer_steps: (i) Nelson Mandela.
(ii) From his comrades in the struggle.
(iii) The triumph over fear.
(iv) Presence.
(v) Conquers.

questions.question:
Read the extract and answer the questions.

*A man who takes away another man's freedom is a prisoner of hatred,*
*he is locked behind the bars of prejudice and narrow-mindedness.*

(i) Who is called 'a prisoner of hatred'?

(ii) What are 'the bars' he is locked behind?

(iii) Name the figure of speech in 'bars of prejudice'.

(iv) What does Mandela conclude from this?

(v) Give a word from the extract meaning 'unfair opinion formed without reason'.
answer_steps: (i) The oppressor, the man who takes away another's freedom.
(ii) Prejudice and narrow-mindedness.
(iii) Metaphor.
(iv) The oppressor must be liberated just as surely as the oppressed.
(v) Prejudice.

questions.question: The inauguration ceremony took place in:
questions.explanation: A sandstone amphitheatre, once the seat of white supremacy.

questions.question: Who was sworn in as first deputy president?
questions.explanation: De Klerk was sworn in first, as second deputy president.

questions.question: Leaders from about how many countries attended?
questions.explanation: It was the largest gathering of international leaders on South African soil.
option_feedback: Leaders came from all over the world.
It was the largest gathering ever.

questions.question: 'Apartheid' means:
options: a system of racial segregation and discrimination
questions.explanation: It separated people by the colour of their skin.
option_feedback: It is a system of oppression.
It was what the movement fought.

questions.question: When was the system of racial domination set up?
options: in the first decade of the twentieth century, after the Anglo-Boer war
questions.explanation: The white-skinned peoples patched up their differences.
option_feedback: It came after the Anglo-Boer war.
It was earlier, in the first decade.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT named by Mandela as a hero of the struggle?
questions.explanation: Mbeki is mentioned as first deputy president, not in the list of heroes.

questions.question: 'Depths of oppression create heights of character' means:
options: great suffering can bring out great qualities in people
questions.explanation: Apartheid produced leaders of courage, wisdom and generosity.

questions.question: According to Mandela, which comes more naturally to the human heart?
questions.explanation: 'If they can learn to hate, they can be taught to love.'
option_feedback: He says people must learn to hate.
He talks of love and hate.
He talks of love and hate.

questions.question: 'Man's goodness is a flame that can be hidden but never extinguished.' Here 'extinguished' means:
questions.explanation: Mandela saw goodness even in prison guards.
option_feedback: It can be hidden but not put out.

questions.question: What did freedom mean to Mandela as a boy?
options: running in the fields, swimming and roasting mealies under the stars
questions.explanation: He felt 'born free' as a boy.
option_feedback: That was as a young man.

questions.question: 'Mealies' are:
questions.explanation: A South African word for maize.

questions.question: 'The chains on any one of my people were the chains on all of them' shows that freedom is:
questions.explanation: No one is free while others are not.
option_feedback: He gave his life for it.

questions.question: What did Mandela's hunger for freedom turn him into?
options: a bold man, a 'criminal' in the eyes of the law and a man without a home
questions.explanation: It changed his whole life.
option_feedback: He gave up a comfortable life.

questions.question: Whom does Mandela call 'a prisoner of hatred'?
questions.explanation: He is locked behind bars of prejudice.
option_feedback: The oppressor is the one ruled by hate.
It is anyone who takes away freedom.
He is speaking of the oppressor.

questions.question: Which anthem did the blacks sing?
questions.explanation: Each group sang the other's anthem.
option_feedback: It was a South African anthem.

questions.question: Mandela calls the end of apartheid:
questions.explanation: 'Never, never and never again...'

questions.question: What is a country's greatest wealth, according to Mandela?
questions.explanation: 'Finer and truer than the purest diamonds.'

questions.question: 'Transitory freedoms' are freedoms that:
questions.explanation: Staying out at night, reading what he pleased.

questions.question: Mandela's 'twin obligations' are to:
questions.explanation: Apartheid made it impossible to fulfil both.
option_feedback: He speaks of family and people.
He speaks of family and people.
He speaks of family and nation.

questions.question: A man of colour who tried to serve his people under apartheid was:
options: torn from his family and forced into secrecy and rebellion
questions.explanation: He lived 'a twilight existence of secrecy and rebellion'.
option_feedback: He was forced to live apart.

questions.question: State whether the following statement is true or false: The generals who saluted Mandela would once have arrested him.
questions.explanation: Not so many years before, they would have arrested him.
option_feedback: Correct! Not so many years before, they would have arrested him.
Not quite. Not so many years before, they would have arrested him.

questions.question: State whether the following statement is true or false: Mandela says the brave man is one who never feels afraid.
questions.explanation: The brave man feels fear but conquers it.
option_feedback: Not quite. The brave man feels fear but conquers it.
Correct! The brave man feels fear but conquers it.

questions.question: State whether the following statement is true or false: As a boy, Mandela felt he was born free.
questions.explanation: He was free to run, swim and play, as long as he obeyed his father and tribal customs.
option_feedback: Correct! He was free to run, swim and play, as long as he obeyed his father and tribal customs.
Not quite. He was free to run, swim and play, as long as he obeyed his father and tribal customs.

questions.question: State whether the following statement is true or false: Mr de Klerk was sworn in as first deputy president.
questions.explanation: He was second deputy president; Thabo Mbeki was first deputy president.
option_feedback: Not quite. He was second deputy president; Thabo Mbeki was first deputy president.
Correct! He was second deputy president; Thabo Mbeki was first deputy president.

questions.question: What did the flypast of jets and helicopters symbolise?
answer_steps: It showed the military's precision and strength.
Above all, it showed the army's loyalty to democracy and to the new, freely elected government.

questions.question: How did Mandela's comrades teach him the meaning of courage?
answer_steps: He saw them risk and give their lives for an idea again and again.
From them he learned that courage is not the absence of fear but the triumph over it.

questions.question: Why could a man of colour not fulfil both his obligations under apartheid?
answer_steps: If he served his people, he was punished and isolated.
He was torn from his family and home and forced into a life of secrecy and rebellion.

questions.question: Trace Mandela's journey from a boy who felt 'born free' to a leader who fought for the freedom of all.
answer_steps: As a boy he enjoyed simple freedoms: running, swimming, roasting mealies, riding bulls.
As a student he wanted to stay out at night and read what he pleased; as a young man he wanted to earn a living and raise a family.
He then realised that his people were not free: 'the chains on any one of my people were the chains on all of them.'
His hunger for freedom made him bold, a 'criminal' in the eyes of the law and a man without a home; he spent years in prison.
Finally he understood that the oppressor too must be freed from hatred; in 1994 he became President to build freedom for all.

questions.question: Mandela believes that love comes more naturally to the human heart than hate. Do you agree? Give reasons from the chapter and from life.
answer_steps: Mandela says no one is born hating; people learn to hate, so they can be taught to love.
Even in prison, a glimpse of humanity in the guards gave him hope; goodness can be hidden but not extinguished.
After 27 years in prison he chose forgiveness, not revenge: the new nation sang both anthems.
In life, children of different backgrounds play together until they are taught prejudice.
So love is natural; hatred is learnt and can be unlearnt.
marking_scheme: 3 marks: content (relevant points from the text)

questions.question: Imagine you attended Mandela's inauguration on 10 May 1994. Write a diary entry describing the day.
answer_steps: Date, place (Union Buildings, Pretoria) and the bright, clear autumn morning.
The oath: de Klerk, Thabo Mbeki and then Mandela; leaders from 140+ countries.
The jets in perfect formation, the generals' salute, and the two anthems sung by both communities.
Your feelings: joy, hope and the sense of history after the end of apartheid.
